Vimian Group AB (VIMIAN-SE) · Investment memo

Vimian: a sound niche compounder whose proven growth is already in the share price, with no EPS upgrades yet in prospect

21 November 2026. Share price SEK 41.80 (EUR 3.80) on 10 November 2026; market value about EUR 2.0bn; enterprise value about EUR 2.3bn. Latest results: the third quarter of 2026, reported on 22 October 2026. Vimian's first Capital Markets Day is on 24 November 2026, three days after this memo, so the memo does not reflect its outcome.

Read every EPS figure on its stated basis
  • EPS before acquisition amortisation is the basis of our model: it leaves out the amortisation of acquired intangibles, about EUR 26m in 2026.
  • EPS after acquisition amortisation deducts that amortisation. Most brokers publish on this second basis, so it is the basis on which to compare our forecast with consensus.
  • The two bases must never be compared with each other. Further notes on the numbers are at the end of the memo.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Vimian is a sound, predictable niche business, and the market has already paid for the proven part of its story. The shares have risen about 40% in six months while consensus EPS for 2027 has not moved.

The good news is proven and priced: the shares are up about 40% in six months on unchanged 2027 EPS estimates.

The unproven part of Vimian's story is whether its growth turns into margin, cash and EPS, and on that question our forecast sits a little below consensus. The business case is good. The skew of EPS revisions over the next 6 to 12 months is not yet favourable, so the shares are not yet the kind of unusually positively skewed bet worth taking at today's price.

The seven key insights:

  1. Vimian's growth is real, broad and the company's own doing. Organic growth was 9%, 12% and 11% in the first three quarters of 2026, while the US clinic-visit market shrank for the eighteenth consecutive quarter. A new chief executive took the weakest unit, MedTech, from -4% to +15% organic growth in five quarters.
  2. Our forecast asks nothing new of the company. Revenue grows 11% to 12% a year (about 8% organic plus bolt-on acquisitions), EBITA about 13% a year and EPS about 16% a year, and free cash flow more than doubles by 2030. About 90% of our EBITA growth to 2028 comes from volume and bolt-ons, the two things Vimian has always delivered.
  3. Consensus asks for something Vimian has not yet shown: operating leverage. Consensus has the EBITDA margin up about 90 basis points in 2027, against our 50 basis points. Like for like, our EPS is about 4% below consensus for 2027 and about 10% below for 2028.
  4. Upgrades are available on revenue and EBITDA, but not on EPS. Brokers model no future acquisitions. Each year of bolt-ons adds about EUR 25m of revenue to estimates when the deals are announced, but almost nothing to EPS after acquisition amortisation.
  5. The costs of buying growth recur between EBITA and EPS, and the market treats them as noise. The costs are acquisition amortisation, earn-out charges, the tax that those charges attract, and the inventory that dental growth needs. These costs are largest when the operating news is best.
  6. The model's return of +42% to March 2028 depends on the guideline fair multiple of 27.07x. The rise in the multiple supplies about a third of that return. With the multiple and the earnings measured on a single EPS basis, the return at 27.07x is +15% to +34%. My own fair multiple is 21x to 24x.
  7. The risks are trackable and the tests are dated. The tests are the Capital Markets Day (24 November 2026), the fourth-quarter report (11 February 2027), the first-quarter report (late April 2027) and the hard comparisons of the second-quarter report (July 2027). Every difference between our forecast and consensus can be checked against a published number.

What would turn the skew favourable: a public cash-and-returns discipline (possible at the Capital Markets Day), a fall in MedTech inventory, a recovery in US orthopaedic volumes, or a share price nearer SEK 30 to 35, where the shares would trade on their median multiple.

The five judgements that move the value of the shares most

Each judgement below shows the base case, a plausible error and the arithmetic of that error. The FY2027 reference points from the model are:

RevenueAdjusted EBITAPre-tax profitNet incomeEPS before acquisition amortisation
EUR 536mEUR 127.4mEUR 107.1mEUR 76.6mEUR 0.144

1. The multiple the market pays in March 2028 is the largest lever on the value of the shares.

  • Base: the guideline fair multiple of 27.07x two-year-forward earnings.
  • Plausible error: the stock's median multiple of 20.2x, which is the multiple of a stock whose progress has stalled.
  • Arithmetic: the model's value of SEK 59.51 a share at 27.07x implies two-year-forward EPS of SEK 2.20, so each turn of the multiple is worth SEK 2.20 a share, or 5.3% of today's price. A fall from 27.07x to 20.2x is 6.9 turns, worth SEK 15.1 a share or 36 points of return. A fall in the multiple of that size has three times the effect of a 12% miss on EPS.

2. Organic growth holds near 8% without help from the market.

  • Base: organic growth of 8.5% in FY2027 and 8.1% in FY2028.
  • Plausible error: organic growth 2 points lower in FY2027, because US orthopaedics turns down or because the allergy franchise loses patients to cheaper itch drugs.
  • Arithmetic: 2 points of growth is EUR 10.7m of revenue, which at a 69% gross margin is EUR 7.4m of gross profit. If costs stay unchanged for two to three quarters, EBITA falls 5.8% and pre-tax profit 6.9%, so EPS falls about 7%, from EUR 0.144 to EUR 0.134. Holding back EUR 5m to 10m of discretionary spending would roughly halve that fall within a year.
  • The upside is smaller than the downside, because Vimian mostly reinvests the profit on extra volume. A recovery in US orthopaedic volumes is worth EUR 2m to 3m of EBITA a year, or 2% to 3% of EPS.

3. The adjusted EBITA margin rises about 30 basis points a year, not the 90 to 100 basis points that consensus has for 2027.

  • Base: an EBITDA margin of 27.4% in FY2027 and 27.6% in FY2028, against consensus of 28.4% and 28.9%.
  • Plausible error: 50 basis points of margin either way.
  • Arithmetic: 0.5% of FY2027 revenue is EUR 2.7m of EBITDA, which is 2.5% of pre-tax profit and therefore 2.5% of EPS. If the consensus margin is right for FY2028, the gap of 1.3 points on revenue of EUR 602m is worth EUR 7.8m. That EUR 7.8m is 6% of pre-tax profit and explains more than half of our 10% gap to consensus EPS for FY2028.

4. The lines between EBITA and EPS behave as modelled. Three items on those lines share one root, the way Vimian pays for its acquisitions.

  • Earn-out charges. Base: EUR 6.5m a year, non-cash. If acquired businesses beat their earn-out measures by 5%, the earn-out liability rises by EUR 5.2m (the company's stated sensitivity is EUR 10.4m for a 10% beat). The charge is not tax-deductible, so net income falls by the full EUR 5.2m, or 6.8%, and EPS before acquisition amortisation falls about 7%. Neither cash in the year nor EPS as most brokers define it changes.
  • Tax. Base: a tax rate of 28.5% in FY2027. If the rate stays at the 31% of the first nine months of 2026, the extra 2.5 points on pre-tax profit of EUR 107.1m cost EUR 2.7m, or 3.5% of EPS.
  • Licensing income from one counterparty, about EUR 10m a year. If the licensing income stopped, at a 60% to 80% margin, EBITA would fall EUR 6m to 8m and EPS 6% to 8%. I think a stop within 18 months is unlikely.

5. Acquisitions stay small, self-funded and priced at about 9x EBITDA.

  • Base: EUR 65m of acquired enterprise value a year. Consensus includes no acquisitions.
  • Arithmetic: EUR 65m at 9x buys EUR 7.2m of EBITDA and about EUR 25m of revenue a year. Funding the deals at about 6% costs EUR 3.9m a year. Each year of deals adds 1% to 2% to EPS before acquisition amortisation and about nothing to EPS after it.
  • With no deals at all, FY2028 revenue would be EUR 38m (6.4%) lower and EBITA EUR 10m lower, with about EUR 6m less interest, so EPS would be about 3% lower.
  • The acquisition error that matters is a large deal funded partly with new shares, which I put at about one chance in seven over 18 months. As an illustration on my own assumptions, a EUR 300m deal at 10x EBITDA, half funded by new shares issued at a 10% discount, adds 8% to the share count and takes net debt to EBITDA from about 1.75x to 2.3x. Such a deal adds about 9% to EPS before acquisition amortisation and about nothing after it. The harm would come through the multiple, as it did after the share issues of 2022 and 2024, which were priced at discounts of 14% and 9.5%.

#1 Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Conclusion: the operating environment is a mild headwind that Vimian has outrun for four quarters; the environment offers no tailwind before 2028, but it also transmits few shocks to Vimian.

Evidence.

  • Vimian's US end market is shrinking in volume. US clinic visits fell 2.2% year on year in the third quarter of 2026 on Vetsource's measure (3.2% on IDEXX's measure), the eighteenth consecutive quarterly fall. Clinics are raising their own prices by 10% to 12% a year, and pet owners are deferring elective care.
  • Vimian's organic growth has run 11 to 14 points ahead of that market in 2026. Most of Vimian's revenue is chronic (allergy immunotherapy), consumable (dental) or membership-based (the VetFamily buying group). Only US orthopaedics, about an eighth of revenue, follows the clinic-visit cycle.
  • A price war in itch drugs is running next to Vimian's allergy business. Zoetis, Elanco and Merck are discounting itch drugs, and Morgan Stanley estimates that Zoetis's net price realisation in companion animals fell 8% in the second half of 2026. The price war has not yet reached Vimian: Specialty Pharma grew 11% underlying in the third quarter, with a higher margin. One new and undated threat is Zoetis's 75-day Cytopoint Plus, licensed on 11 November 2026, which narrows the convenience advantage of Vimian's immunotherapy.
  • Regulation is mostly helpful. The US excluded animal health from its tariffs on imported drugs, and the UK competition remedies stop at the clinic. US tariffs on imported medical devices are still undecided and would cost Vimian EUR 1.5m to 4m of EBITA before mitigation.
  • Currency is a steady drag. The US dollar accounts for 38% of revenue and is unhedged. A 10% move in the dollar changes revenue by EUR 15.7m and EBIT by EUR 2.3m. The base case assumes 1.4 points of currency translation drag on revenue growth in 2027.
  • The slow positives are real but undated. The pets acquired during 2020 to 2022 are reaching the ages of chronic care, and dental disease in pets is under-treated. The separation of DePuy Synthes from Johnson & Johnson may distract Vimian's main orthopaedic rival, although clinicians interviewed in September 2026 said the separation would not change their choice of supplier.

Inference. The operating environment is a mild net headwind, worth one to two points of organic growth, with a negative tail and no dated relief. Vimian's growth is therefore the company's own work, and that independence cuts both ways. Industry shocks reach Vimian weakly and late, which helps predictability, but nothing external will supply upgrades either.

So what. The base case assumes no market recovery before 2028. US orthopaedics is the one cyclical option in the case, and a recovery there would be upside. The early-warning indicator for a spill-over of the itch-drug price war is Specialty Pharma's underlying growth: a reading below 8% would be the first sign.

Against the market. I agree with the sell-side that Vimian's niches are insulated from the market, because four quarters of data show the insulation. I differ on what consensus revenue requires. Consensus revenue growth of 11.5% for 2027 contains only 1.7 points of carry-over from 2026 acquisitions and no new deals, so consensus implies organic growth of 10% to 11%. Without a recovery in US orthopaedics, which neither management nor the data supports, that implied organic growth is about two points too high. Some brokers have hoped for relief from lower interest rates, but the data show no such relief.

Counter-case. The turn in the US clinic market may be nearer than I assume. IDEXX grew its recurring revenue 11% in the third quarter and cited ageing pets and more frequent testing as the cause. If elective demand returns, the US field sales force that Vimian installed in January 2026 gives it real leverage to the recovery. After 2008, same-store clinic volumes took eleven quarters to turn positive, and the current slump is already 18 quarters old.

What would change my view.

  • Two consecutive quarters of positive US clinic-visit growth, or management describing US orthopaedics as growing at mid-single digits.
  • A gross margin below 68%, or Specialty Pharma's underlying growth below 6% for two quarters.

Score: 41, set by the Rater. The external balance is a mild net headwind of one to two organic points: US clinic visits have fallen for 18 quarters, a price war in itch drugs runs next door (with Zoetis's new 75-day Cytopoint Plus as a direct threat to immunotherapy), the unhedged dollar drags 1.4 points in 2027 and device tariffs are undecided, while the slow positives (ageing pandemic pets, under-treated dental disease) are real but undated; chronic, consumable and membership revenue keeps the transmission weak, so the score sits just below the group's 42 and just below Carlsberg's mature but modest environment, above Entra's rate-driven negative.

#2 Internally driven corporate change

Conclusion: Vimian's internal change is strong and proven on growth, but the change has yet to reach margin, cash and capital allocation, which is where the next leg of the case must come from.

Evidence.

  • The leadership layer was rebuilt in sixteen months. The board, on which the controlling shareholder Fidelio Capital sits, removed the previous chief executive in July 2025. Alireza Tajbakhsh, who built VetFamily, became permanent chief executive on 24 November 2025. New heads arrived in MedTech (April 2026), Specialty Pharma (1 October 2026) and acquisitions (5 October 2026). The chief financial officer was released from a second role in October 2026 to concentrate on cash and capital allocation.
  • The commercial response was fast. MedTech moved to a US field sales force, cut 4,000 of its 22,000 product lines and ended its annual order programme. Organic growth and adjusted EBITA have beaten consensus for three consecutive quarters.
  • The acquisition engine is active and disciplined on price. About 80% of deals are bilateral, at about 9x EBITDA. Acquisition spending of EUR 80m to 95m a year in 2024 to 2026 left leverage at 2.0x on the company's measure, against a ceiling of 3.0x. The latest deal, Norfolk Medical Products, takes the surgeons who use Movora's implants into soft-tissue surgery.
  • The change has not reached the group margin. The adjusted EBITA margin was 24.3% in the third quarter of 2026, against 24.5% a year earlier, and central costs rose 67%.
  • The change has not reached capital allocation either. Management incentives pay on absolute adjusted EBITA (70%) and revenue (30%), with no return or cash measure. Vimian pays no dividend and buys back no shares. The group's perimeter is widening, most oddly into Italian pet cremation, and the group has no internal audit function across its operations in about 80 countries.
  • Cash conversion is weak, but the cause is narrower than it first looked. Operating cash flow was about half of adjusted EBITDA in the first nine months of 2026. Nearly all of the 2026 rise in receivables came with acquired businesses: organic receivables rose only about EUR 1.5m while organic revenue grew about 11%. The organic build in working capital is about EUR 17m of MedTech inventory, mainly dental stock. Net working capital is 25% of revenue, against the company's planned level of about 23%.
  • One profit stream depends on one counterparty. Specialty Pharma earns about EUR 10m a year of licensing income from an entity owned by the founder of Bova, the compounding business Vimian bought in 2022. The entity holds pharmacy licences that a company cannot hold directly in some jurisdictions. Vimian describes the licensing terms as arm's length.

Inference. Vimian has undergone a genuine major corporate change in people and commercial execution, and the change has reached revenue and segment profit but not yet group margin, cash or capital allocation. The change still needed is a cash-and-returns discipline. That discipline is what separates the decentralised acquirers that compound value from those that do not (#3).

So what. The next leg of the case needs a second change, and the Capital Markets Day on 24 November 2026 is the first occasion on which Vimian could announce one.

A public working-capital or return target is the single change that would most improve the case, and the Capital Markets Day on 24 November is the first chance for Vimian to set one.

The working-capital problem is fixable. The problem is one segment's inventory, which Vimian publishes each quarter and which the company has reduced before (by EUR 8m in one quarter of 2023).

Against the market. The market narrative is "growth proven, margins the next test", and brokers expect Vimian to pass the margin test.

Where I agree with the market

The change is real and management deserves the credit: the old team missed in a weak 2025, and the new team beat in an equally weak 2026.

Where I differ, in two directions

Less convinced on margin: a decentralised model with thirteen people at the centre has no mechanism for operating leverage.

More constructive on cash: receivables normalised as the company said they would, and the remaining problem, MedTech inventory, is specific and fixable.

Counter-case. The new chief executive grew VetFamily with rising margins, and one broker calls his record "highly solid". Four quarters is a short sample, but every reading points the same way. If investment spending plateaus, the group margin could follow growth with a lag of about a year.

What would change my view.

  • A public cash-conversion, working-capital or return-on-capital target; a return measure in the incentive plan; or inventory at or below EUR 98m at the year-end.
  • A large or equity-funded acquisition, or further drift of the group's perimeter into unrelated businesses.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. A genuine, fast reset of people and commercial execution (new chief executive, new heads of MedTech, Specialty Pharma and acquisitions; MedTech from -4% to +15% organic in five quarters; three consecutive EBITA beats; a disciplined bilateral bolt-on engine at about 9x EBITDA) is a large change force, but the reset has not reached the group margin (24.3% against 24.5%, central costs +67%), cash (operating cash about half of EBITDA, EUR 17m of dental inventory) or capital allocation (no return measure in pay, no audit function, drift into pet cremation); I sit a little above the group's 60 because the growth evidence is already in four quarters, and below OEM International because its change has already lifted the margin to a record.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Conclusion: strong niche positions and an above-average profile on growth and gross margin are held back by average returns on capital, weak cash conversion and governance built for scale more than for value per share.

Evidence.

  • Value chain. Vimian sits in the two best stages of the animal-health value chain, specialty product intellectual property and group purchasing, each earning about 28% at the operating line in the research's map of the chain. Vimian's gross margin is 68.9%.
  • Niche leadership. Vimian is number one or two in four niches: veterinary orthopaedics (Movora, with about 40% of North American implants, twice its nearest rival), dental (iM3), allergy immunotherapy (Nextmune) and buying groups (VetFamily, with 12,400 clinics in 14 markets). Vimian is marginal in diagnostics, where IDEXX holds 72% of point-of-care equipment.
  • Industry structure. Vimian is under 1% of a USD 50bn industry in which five companies hold about 70%. The giants compete on blockbuster drugs and ignore Vimian's niches. Vimian's customers are consolidating faster than its competitors: corporate groups own about 30% of US general practices and 60% to 80% of UK practices.
  • Moats. Vimian's moats are mostly switching costs: surgeons trained on Movora's instrument sets (48,000 professionals educated in 2025), lifelong immunotherapy prescribed from Vimian's own allergy tests, dental equipment that pulls through consumables, and rebate tiers in the buying group. Product registrations slow new entrants. Cross-selling between Vimian's units is about 18% of sales and about a third of Specialty Pharma's organic growth.
  • Financial profile: above average on growth and margin, and average or worse on returns and cash. The two figures below set out the evidence. Between 2023 and 2025 the adjusted EBITA margin fell from 26.3% to 24.8% while revenue grew 28%.
  • Management. Judged by his actions, the chief executive is an enabler, and he owns shares on a founder-like scale (426,000 directly, plus incentive shares). His goal of adjusted EBITA above EUR 300m by 2030 is stretching to a fault (#4). The strategy is coherent: bilateral bolt-ons, dental as the anchor of MedTech, direct sales in place of distributors, companion-animal diagnostics and cross-selling. The strategy is, however, a growth strategy with no capital-return discipline attached. The culture is decentralised and entrepreneurial, and that culture is what sources the bilateral deals. Fidelio owns 58.4% of the shares and chairs the acquisitions committee.

Inference. Vimian is a high-quality collection of niche businesses inside a medium-quality financial structure. The moats protect growth and gross margin, and the acquisition model then pays away much of their value through goodwill, earn-outs and amortisation. Vimian's competitive position rests more on specialisation, and on being too small to attract a giant's attention, than on dominance.

So what. The business merits a valuation for durable organic growth of about 8% and segment margins of 25% to 30%, but it does not yet merit a compounder's premium. The Nordic acquirers that earn a compounder's premium share a feature Vimian lacks: an explicit return-on-working-capital rule imposed on every subsidiary. Addtech reports a return on working capital of 82%, and Indutrade converts more than 130% of profit into cash. The animal-health evidence points the same way. IDEXX trades on 48x 2027 earnings for recurring revenue and high returns, while Vetoquinol delivered its margin plan and sits at the bottom of its valuation range because it does not grow. The market pays for growth and cash conversion together.

Against the market. One broker argues that Vimian's discount to the Nordic compounders is unwarranted and will close as Vimian's record lengthens. I think the discount reflects returns and cash discipline more than the length of the record, so time alone will not close it. Another broker has described the group as a "loose collection of assets"; on that point I am more positive, because the cross-selling figures show that the assets work together.

Counter-case. Return on tangible capital is high, on my estimate 40% to 55%, so the underlying businesses are excellent and the gap to reported returns is the price of past deals. Organic profit growth now accrues on a fixed goodwill base, which lifts return on invested capital towards 10% to 12% by 2028. Financial buyers prize such assets: EQT paid 26x EBIT for Dechra in 2023.

What would change my view.

  • A credible path to a 15% return on invested capital, which needs margin and working capital to improve together.
  • A large company choosing to enter one of Vimian's four niches, or evidence that corporate clinic groups are using tenders to cut implant and dental prices.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Qualitatively good units in an ordinary whole: number one or two in four niches (Movora about 40% of North American implants, iM3, Nextmune, VetFamily's 12,400 clinics) with switching-cost moats, a 69% gross margin and organic growth above the market every year since 2021, but the position rests on specialisation and obscurity next to giants, and the financial profile is weak on returns and cash (reported ROIC 9.4% on EUR 590m of goodwill, 3.3% on the Universe basis at the 26th percentile; bolt-ons at 9x EBITDA earn about the cost of capital after amortisation; only 30% of adjusted EBITA reaching net income; margin down from 26.3% to 24.8%) under sponsor-first governance with abandoned targets; coherent with the groups (51, 53, 39, 43), the score sits just below Shell's mid-cycle quality and above Xvivo's one-moat business.

#4 Guidance, expectation management and the record of delivery

Conclusion: Vimian's guidance is conservative for the next two quarters and unrealistic for 2030, and there is no annual guidance to raise, so upgrades can come only from results and deals.

Evidence.

  • There is no annual guidance to raise. Vimian's one public target is adjusted EBITA above EUR 300m by 2030, "over half organic", with "no further capital injections" and leverage below 3.0x. Vimian reaffirmed the target on 22 October 2026. Our 2030 forecast for adjusted EBITA is EUR 190m, so the target is 58% above our forecast. On the research's arithmetic, the target needs about three times the present pace of acquisitions, or new equity.
  • Vimian's longer record is of targets set high and then dropped: a 35% margin, a 30% sales growth rate, and EUR 200m of adjusted EBITA by 2025 (actual: EUR 105m).
  • The new chief executive frames each quarter cautiously and then beats it. He called the first quarter of 2026 "transitional", and adjusted EBITA came in 3% ahead of consensus. The second and third quarters were each 4% ahead.
  • Management's near-term signals match our forecast inputs line by line: US orthopaedics growing at low single digits, the Veterinary Services margin normalising to about 28.5%, the Diagnostics margin improving "from 2027", and capital spending of about 4% of revenue.
  • One management signal is not conservative. Management speaks of "maintaining double-digit organic growth", and consensus revenue now embeds that growth rate (#1).
  • Vimian does not manage expectations below EBITA. Consensus EPS for 2026 fell 15% over the same twelve months in which the company beat consensus three times. Over twelve months, consensus for 2027 shows sales up 7%, EBITDA up 4% and EPS down 7%.

Inference. Vimian is not a company with conservative guidance and a habit of raising it. Vimian has no annual guidance, a recent habit of beating the quarter, and one long-term target that will have to change.

So what. Upgrades must come from results and from announced deals, because guidance cannot supply them. The quarterly beat at the operating level should keep working for two more quarters, because the comparisons are easy and cautious framing sets a low bar. The beat weakens from the second quarter of 2027, when I expect organic growth of about 7% against 12% a year earlier. I put the chance that management drops the "double-digit" wording by then at about three in four.

Against the market. Brokers are split on the 2030 target, from "requires flawless execution" to supportive. I go further than the sceptics: the target cannot be met on its stated terms, and I put the chance that Vimian re-dates or drops the target by late 2029 at about 55%. I agree with the market that the near-term tone is conservative and that the next two quarters are more likely than not to beat consensus at the EBITA line.

Counter-case. A former group controller calls the 2030 target "ambitious but not impossible", and the board may have a platform deal in view. More usefully, if the Capital Markets Day sets segment corridors with this chief executive's usual caution, they would be the first Vimian targets with a fair chance of being met, and a record of raising and beating targets could start there.

What would change my view. A margin corridor by segment, an acquisition envelope, a cash target and a view of tax and earn-out payments would move this topic up sharply. The cautionary precedent is Swedencare, which set five-year targets at its first capital markets day in June 2026, missed the next quarter and lost its chief executive by September.

Score: 39, set by the Rater. The two-to-three-year record weighs heavily: the 35% margin, 30% growth and EUR 200m 2025 EBITA targets were all dropped (actual EUR 105m), consensus EPS for 2026 fell 15% in the same twelve months in which the company beat, and the reaffirmed 2030 target of EUR 300m sits 58% above the model and is likely to be re-dated, while the de facto 'double-digit organic' steer is not conservative; against that, the new chief executive's cautious framing has produced three quarters of 3-4% EBITA beats, which lifts the score above the groups' 28 and 35 but leaves the company below Instalco, which has a similar miss-then-beat pattern without an unachievable live target.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Conclusion: pricing power defends Vimian's margin and financial leverage adds a few points to EPS growth, but operating leverage is weak by design, so Vimian's model does not turn revenue growth into outsized operating profit growth.

Evidence, lever by lever.

The levers that defend or help

  • Pricing power is applied, and it defends the margin. Vimian has taken price rises of about 5% and passed on wage inflation. The gross margin has held at 68.9% for two years while input costs rose about 13% a year. In our forecast, price contributes three to four points of organic growth and adds nothing to margin.
  • Financial leverage does help EPS. Net financial items fall from EUR 24.5m in 2026 to EUR 20m to 21m a year and then stay flat while EBITA grows, so they shrink from about 21% of adjusted EBITA in 2026 to about 14% in 2028. Together with a lower tax rate, the flat financial items let EPS grow about three points a year faster than EBITA. Net debt to EBITDA falls from 1.8x to 1.2x by 2030 on the model's basis, after EUR 70m a year of deals.
  • The commercial feedback loops reinforce revenue. Each bolt-on adds a product to sell into 17,000 clinics. Training leads to installed instruments, which lead to consumables. More buying-group members earn better rebates, which attract more members.

The levers that are weak

  • Operating leverage is low by design. Vimian's units are autonomous and its manufacturing is outsourced. Incremental adjusted EBITA margins were 19% over 2023 to 2025 and 22% in the first nine months of 2026, against an average margin near 25%. In the third quarter of 2026 revenue rose 15% and adjusted EBITA 14%. Our base case implies an incremental margin of about 27%; consensus implies 36% for 2027.
  • The operating leverage that exists is asymmetric. A revenue shortfall hits the margin at once, while Vimian mostly reinvests the profit on extra volume. Genuine fixed-cost leverage sits only in the US field sales force and the two consolidated Diagnostics sites, together worth EUR 3m to 5m by 2028.
  • Cost scope is small. Identifiable savings are EUR 2m to 4m, and Vimian is likely to reinvest most of them.

The loops that dampen earnings and cash

  • The financial feedback loops dampen earnings and cash. The better the acquired businesses perform, the larger the earn-out revaluation charge (EUR 4.5m in the first nine months of 2026) and the higher the tax rate (35% in the first quarter). The maximum earn-out payout has risen to EUR 142m, against EUR 32m carried on the balance sheet. Growth also ties up 28 to 30 cents of working capital per euro of extra revenue, so free cash flow is only 27% of EBITDA in 2026, rising to 42% by 2030.
  • Reported EBITDA flatters the trend. Capitalised development doubled to EUR 7.7m in the first nine months of 2026. Between 2025 and 2026 the adjusted EBITA margin falls 30 basis points while the EBITDA margin rises 20 basis points, and consensus is expressed in EBITDA.

Inference. Vimian's revenue growth produces roughly proportionate EBITA growth. EPS growth is outsized, but through the lines below EBITA and not through operations. Dental, about a tenth of the group, shows how the loops connect, because dental runs through five lines at once: MedTech growth and margin (positive), and inventory, earn-out charges and tax (all negative). Within the 18-month window, a better dental outcome raises EBITA and lowers free cash flow and reported EPS in the same period.

So what: judge each quarterly report on adjusted EBITA. A beat on EBITA with disappointing EPS and cash can be the same good news. An EBITDA beat with a flat EBITA margin is not operating leverage. Because the earn-out charge dampens EPS in both directions, a strong EPS print can mean that acquired businesses are missing their earn-out targets.

Against the market. Consensus has the EBITDA margin up about 170 basis points between 2025 and 2027, and the bullish argument is that margins will expand "as investments plateau". I expect the adjusted EBITA margin to rise about 30 basis points a year. Jefferies, at 24.9% for 2027, is the broker nearest to us, and our forecast is just below Jefferies at 24.8%. The market also treats earn-out charges as noise, whereas I think they are a recurring cost tied to success.

Counter-case. MedTech earned a 27.1% margin at its best, against 24.4% now. Diagnostics could move from a 7% margin to the mid-teens, and Veterinary Services is running above 30%. If all three improvements came through in one year, a group margin gain of 100 basis points is achievable, and the new team has not yet had a full year to try.

What would change my view. An adjusted EBITA margin of 25.3% or more for 2027 (reported in February 2028), or two consecutive quarters in which EBITA grows three points faster than revenue.

Score: 38, set by the Rater. Pricing power is real but defensive (about 5% price taken, gross margin held at 68.9% against 13% a year input inflation, but adding nothing to margin), operating leverage is low by design and asymmetric (incremental adjusted EBITA margins of 19-22% against an average near 25%, extra volume reinvested, a shortfall hits at once, cost scope only EUR 2-4m), and the financial loops dampen profits (earn-out charges and tax rise with success, 28-30 cents of working capital per euro of revenue); only falling interest and tax lift EPS about three points above EBITA, so EPS growth of about 16% on revenue growth of 11.6% is about 1.4 times, against the Universe's typical 2 times, placing the score between the 50 level's asymmetric leverage and the 25 level's profit growing in line with revenue, consistent with the Economic strength group's 39.

Evidence and inference.

  • Double-digit growth on every line is well founded. From 2026 to 2030, revenue compounds at 11.6% a year, EBITDA and adjusted EBITA at about 12.7%, and EPS at about 16%.

Revenue grew 13% to 18% a year in 2023 to 2025 on larger deals, but adjusted EBITA grew only about 10% a year because the margin fell, and EPS on the brokers' basis grew about 9% a year. In the forecast the margin stops falling and less profit is lost below EBITA.
  • The margin recovers, modestly. The adjusted EBITA margin gains 100 basis points from the 2026 trough and in 2030 is still below its 2023 level. The gain comes from Diagnostics (a margin rising from 9% to 15%) and MedTech (from 25% to 27%), less the normalisation of Veterinary Services and higher central costs.
  • The forecast leans on the reliable lines. Of the EBITA growth from 2026 to 2028, about 60% comes from organic volume at a constant margin, about 30% from bolt-ons and about 10% from margin.
  • Free cash flow roughly equals acquisition spending, so net debt stays near EUR 240m to 265m and leverage falls only through growth in EBITDA. The base case assumes no release of working capital. Each point of revenue held in working capital is EUR 5.4m, a tenth of 2027 free cash flow.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Conclusion: price and narrative momentum are strong and company-specific, estimate momentum is only middling and peers' momentum is weak, so the share price has run ahead of the numbers.

Evidence.

  • Price momentum: strong. The shares are up 39.6% in six months and 44.5% in twelve months. They rank in the 94th percentile of relative strength, trade 33% above their 200-day average and sit within 2% of their 52-week high. The dashboard rates technical momentum B and thematic momentum B.
  • Estimate momentum: middling. The dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum C. Target prices are up 6% in a month and 11% in six months. The share of buy ratings is unchanged at 57% (three Buys, two Holds and a Sell), and the mean target price is just below the share price.
  • Guidance momentum: none. Vimian cannot upgrade guidance because it gives none, and it reaffirmed the 2030 target rather than raising it.
  • Narrative momentum: strong. The narrative moved from a broken roll-up with a leadership vacuum in February 2026 to "Growth Proven, Margins the Next Test" (Jefferies) and "Another beat builds confidence" (DNB Carnegie) by October.
  • The share-price rise is a rise in the multiple. The two-year-forward P/E went from 17.9x at the end of May 2026 to 25.2x, while the 2027 EPS estimate stayed flat.
  • The momentum is Vimian's own. A basket of 33 European peers explains only 7% of the daily variance of Vimian's share price, and the stock's beta to that basket is 0.45.
  • Peer momentum: weak. Vetoquinol, Virbac and Genus sit at the 1st, 5th and 12th percentiles of their own ten-year valuation ranges, with earnings momentum rated D, C and F. Swedencare missed its third quarter and is losing its chief executive. Zoetis fell 6% on its third-quarter report. IDEXX rose 19% on its own results, and that rise did not lift the smaller Nordic names.

Inference. A re-rating of about 40% on flat estimates means the market is paying in advance for Vimian's conversion of growth into margin, cash and EPS.

So what. The momentum is an asset while Vimian's reports support it, and the next two reports should. Because the momentum is company-specific, sector strength will not extend it, and sector weakness has not held it back. The momentum is not a defensive property: in the stressed market of spring 2025, Vimian's beta was about 1.0. The present market regime buys healthcare as a defensive sector but marks down small, leveraged, acquisition-led companies first, which helps the sector more than it helps Vimian.

Against the market. I read the facts as the market does; the difference is one of interpretation. The market narrative reads the rise as recognition of proven growth. I read most of the rise as payment for a margin recovery that estimates already contain and that our forecast puts lower.

Counter-case. Stocks that rise on their own news while their reports keep beating often run further than valuation suggests, and three brokers' targets are above the share price.

What would change my view. EPS revisions turning positive over six months, or peers re-rating, would strengthen Vimian's momentum. A weak share-price reaction to an operating beat would be the first sign of the momentum fading, as after the second quarter of 2026, when poor cash flow tempered the response.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. Both measures positive and none strongly negative gives B: price momentum is top-decile (up 40% in six months, 33% above the 200-day average, near the high) and the narrative has moved from 'broken roll-up' to 'growth proven', but consensus 2027 EPS is +3% over three months and -1% over six (38th percentile), Buy ratings are unchanged at 57%, there is no guidance to raise (not negative) and peers are weak (not counted against it); placed just above mid-band because the re-rating has run on flat estimates.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Conclusion: the operating forecasts are simple and trackable, but EPS is clouded by its definitions and by acquisition accounting, and the share price carries the risks of a thin float and a high multiple, which could bite suddenly.

Evidence.

  • The operating case is simple. The operating case is 8% organic growth, bolt-ons and a small margin gain, across four segments and 17,000 clinics, with no customer above 10% of revenue. In the weak year of 2025, with US orthopaedics shrinking, the group still grew 6% organically and adjusted EBITA rose 11%. The 2025 result is a fair picture of the downside for the business.
  • The earnings case is not simple. Eight lines sit between segment EBITA and EPS, and the company gives no forward view of any of them. Brokers' "adjusted" EPS for 2026 runs from EUR 0.089 to EUR 0.140, and that 57% spread is one of definition, not of forecasting.
  • The range of outcomes widens down the profit and loss account. For FY2027, I expect the following bands to hold about two times in three: revenue within 4% of our base, adjusted EBITA within 7%, EPS within 12% and free cash flow within 25%.
  • Each view of the future requires something different. Our base case requires nothing the company has not already done. Consensus requires operating leverage. The 2030 target requires three times the present pace of deals, or new equity.
  • Most risks are gradual and published quarterly: the slowdown against hard comparisons, the margin, MedTech inventory, earn-out charges and the licensing income.
  • A few risks would be sudden:

  • Share-price risk is larger than earnings risk. On unchanged earnings, a return to the stock's five-year median multiple would put the shares 16% below today's price, the lower quartile 27% below and the bottom decile about 40% below. The shares traded at SEK 27 to 28 as recently as May 2026.
  • The float is thin. The free float is one third to 40% of the shares, and about USD 2.4m of shares trade a day. A placing of 5% of the company would equal about 57 days of average volume (my arithmetic, on the dashboard's three-month volume).
  • Precedents show a sector that is resilient in value but harsh on individual franchises. Pet spending grew through past US downturns, yet listed acquirers valued on adjusted earnings de-rate quickly when organic growth or cash disappoints:

Inference. Fundamental risk is moderate and mostly gradual, while price risk is high and can be sudden. The risk in this case lies in conversion and in the share price, not in the business.

So what. The case can be tracked closely, which is the constructive point. Read each report in this order: segment organic growth; adjusted EBITA; inventory and operating cash flow; and only then EPS, on a stated basis. The thresholds to watch in the fourth-quarter report on 11 February 2027 are:

  • fourth-quarter organic growth of about 10%;
  • a group margin of about 24.2% or better;
  • inventory at or below EUR 98m;
  • operating cash flow of about EUR 21m in the quarter;
  • earn-out probability adjustments below EUR 3m.
The risks are trackable: every difference between our forecast and consensus can be checked against a published number on 11 February 2027.

Against the market. Jefferies calls the risk and reward "balanced", and the controlling holder is generally described as a source of stability.

Operating risk: lower than the market thinks

Operating risk is lower than the last five years imply, because the business is larger and more spread, and leverage is half its 2022 peak.

Price risk: higher than the market thinks

Price risk is higher than the narrative allows, because the multiple has risen by about 40% on unchanged estimates (#8).

Counter-case. Price risk may be lower than I think. There are no disclosed short positions, the register is long-only, Fidelio has supported every capital raise, and Jefferies considers a block sale improbable in the medium term.

What would change my view.

  • Lower risk: a public cash-and-returns discipline and a fall in inventory.
  • Higher risk: a large deal, a second quarter of cash flow as weak as the second quarter of 2026, or any disturbance to the licensing income.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple and trackable (8% organic growth, bolt-ons, four segments, no customer above 10%, a 2025 downside of +6% organic), but the memo's FY2027 EPS band is only about +/-12% at two-in-three confidence, eight undisclosed lines sit between segment EBITA and EPS with broker definitions spanning 57%, and share-price risk is high and sudden (a multiple up about 40% on flat estimates, 16-40% above its median-to-decile levels, a thin float under a 58% holder with no lock-up, a one-in-seven large equity-funded deal, a single-counterparty licence worth 6-8% of EPS), in a sector that de-rates acquirers fast when organic growth or cash disappoints; between the groups' 42 and 52, the score sits below IMCD's simple but levered distribution case and just above Rexel's.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: Vimian is in the Reinforcing phase but late in it, and stalling during 2027 is the most likely next step unless evidence of conversion arrives.

Evidence.

  • The dashboard's rule places the stock in the Reinforcing phase.
  • The sequence of events fits the Reinforcing phase. The stock bottomed between February and May 2026 at SEK 27 to 28 and turned up with the second-quarter report in July. The thesis broadened with the third quarter, when three of the four segments grew at double digits and target prices rose. The stock now sits near its high, with a narrative of "growth proven".
  • The Reinforcing phase continues only while upgrades continue. On our forecast, revenue upgrades arrive with deals, but EPS estimates are trimmed from mid-2027 (#7).
  • Headline organic growth slows from 12% to about 7% by the second quarter of 2027, before any proof of margin conversion can arrive. That proof comes only with the full-year report in February 2028.

Inference. The stock is late in the Reinforcing phase, and its more likely next phase is Stalling. Collapsing is unlikely, because the operating case is too well spread and too well evidenced.

So what. The lifecycle phase sets the guideline multiple. The Reinforcing phase earns the top decile of the stock's historical multiple range, but a stock that is late in Reinforcing and at risk of stalling earns less (#11).

Against the market. I agree with the dashboard on where the stock is today, but I differ on how long it stays there. The market narrative assumes that conversion follows growth on schedule. I expect a gap of two to three quarters in mid-2027 in which growth slows and conversion is not yet visible.

Counter-case. The next two reports face easy comparisons (organic growth of 6% and 9% a year earlier). A deal, or modelled building blocks from the Capital Markets Day, could extend the Reinforcing phase through mid-2027, by which time US orthopaedics may have turned.

What would change my view. A cash or return target on 24 November, a rising group margin in the fourth and first quarters, or rising estimates for 2027 EBITDA after the second-quarter report would keep the stock in the Reinforcing phase.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The computed and memo phase of Reinforcing is right but late: the stock bottomed at SEK 27-28, turned in July and broadened in the third quarter, and the good news is now known, with the next two reports supportive on easy comparisons but organic growth halving to about 7% by the second quarter of 2027 before margin proof can arrive, so the memo's 50% chance of Stalling and 15% of Collapsing within twelve months outweigh 35% of continued Reinforcing; that places the score below Solid State's early turn and a little above Linea Directa's unrecognised Bottoming.

Evidence.

  • The guideline. For a stock in the Reinforcing phase, the guideline fair multiple is the 90th percentile of the stock's own history of two-year-forward P/E, and the model uses 27.07x. The shares trade on about 25.2x, in the top quarter of their five-year range. The dashboard rates valuation C on a different measure, the current P/E of 21.0x, which is at the 57th percentile of its history.
  • The history is short and its top is thin. The history covers 64 months since the 2021 listing. Since mid-2022 the multiple has been at or above 27x at only five of 52 month-ends (August to November 2024 and May 2025), when the shares traded at SEK 43 to 47. Each of those episodes was followed within a year by a fall to about 18x.
  • The EPS basis matters. The multiple history is measured on consensus EPS, which is mostly after acquisition amortisation. On our own EPS after acquisition amortisation, the shares already trade on about 30x.
  • What the sell-side pays. Jefferies' target of SEK 40 is 19x 2027 EV to EBIT, and Jefferies says the shares "already price in a recovery". DNB Carnegie's target of SEK 45 is 17x 2027 EV to EBITA, a 10% premium to the animal-health peers (15.7x) and the Nordic compounders (15.4x) that DNB Carnegie compares Vimian with. On our own EBITA forecast, the shares already trade on about 17x (my arithmetic).
  • A cross-check. DNB Carnegie's SEK 45 is the highest named target. If the shares reached SEK 45 in twelve months, they would trade on about 23x two-year-forward earnings at that date, assuming consensus EPS grows as forecast (my arithmetic).

My view. A multiple of 27x is the multiple of peak delivery with EPS upgrades. Vimian is delivering on revenue but has yet to deliver on EPS and cash. Its return on invested capital is about 10%, it returns no cash to shareholders, and I expect the stock to move from Reinforcing towards Stalling. I therefore put the fair multiple at 21x to 24x, between the stock's median (20.2x) and its upper quartile (23.5x to 23.8x), and a little below today's level. The guideline's 27x becomes fair once Vimian shows conversion; until then 27x is the multiple of the bull case.

So what. At a fair multiple of 21x to 24x, the fall from today's multiple absorbs a good part of the next 18 months of earnings growth (#12).

Against the market. My range is close to what the brokers' targets imply, since the mean target is about today's price. Applied to earnings 18 months ahead, as the model applies it, the guideline multiple gives a value above every broker's target.

Counter-case. Proven Nordic compounders trade above 18x EBITA, and one of them on 34x earnings, for organic growth below Vimian's. If Vimian adopts their discipline, 27x is not stretched for a business compounding EBITA at about 13% a year. A thin float can also sustain a scarcity premium for a long time.

What would change my view.

  • Towards the guideline: a public return discipline, together with a rising margin in the 2027 accounts.
  • Towards the median: organic growth below 7%.

What drives each part of the return.

  • Dividends and other cash returns: nil. All free cash flow, EUR 51m to 88m a year, goes into bolt-ons of about EUR 70m a year, so the return comes entirely from the share price.
  • Earnings: +24.8%, which is 18 months of EPS growth at about 16% a year. Today's two-year-forward EPS covers the year to September 2028 (about EUR 0.160). In March 2028, the two-year-forward EPS will cover the year to March 2030 (about EUR 0.200). The earnings part of the return therefore rests on 2029 and 2030, for which only one broker publishes an estimate today.
  • The 16% EPS growth rests mostly on volume and bolt-ons. In a typical forecast year, revenue growth contributes about 11.7 points (7.6 organic and 4.2 from bolt-ons), the margin 1.7 points, financial items staying flat while profit grows 2.2 points, and a lower tax rate about 1 point, less dilution (my arithmetic on FY2029). Organic volume and bolt-ons supply roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of the EPS growth.
  • The multiple: +14.1%, from 23.7x to 27.07x. The multiple is the weak part of the calculation. The starting 23.7x is today's price on the model's EPS before acquisition amortisation, whereas the 27.07x comes from a history measured on consensus EPS, on which the shares trade at 25.1x today. The difference of basis also explains why the dashboard's valuation-based return rating (F) and the model's return disagree. The multiple is the largest lever: each turn is worth SEK 2.20 a share, or about 5 points of return.

Sensitivity to the multiple (#11). At an exit multiple of 23.5x, the return to March 2028 is about nil to +17% on the two like-for-like bases. At the median multiple of 20.2x, the return is about -14% to nil.

The skew of outcomes, on my judgement.

Outcome by March 2028ProbabilityMultipleReturn
Conversion shows: consensus margins are met and cash improves35%The guideline, 27xAbout +30% to +40%

Weighted by these probabilities, the expected return is about +10% to March 2028. The upside case needs evidence that is not yet in hand, whereas the middle case needs only our base forecast.

Against the market. Brokers' targets run from about SEK 29 to about SEK 50, with a mean near SEK 41, and none is near the model's SEK 59.5. The difference between the brokers and the model is almost entirely the multiple and the EPS basis. The difference is not the earnings forecast, where we are below consensus.

Counter-case. Serial acquirers are commonly valued on earnings before acquisition amortisation, as DNB Carnegie values Vimian. If the market moves to that basis and awards Vimian a compounder's multiple, the model's +42% is the right figure.

What would change my view. The Financial Analyst restating the guideline multiple on one EPS basis; brokers converging on one EPS definition; or the evidence of conversion listed in #10.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. About +10% sits on the C/D boundary and maps to about 50, entirely share price with no dividend; the lower tail (15% at -20% to -35%) is a little fatter than the base case's -5% to +10% suggests, but the three-year figure of +40% to +62% at the guideline multiple on a single basis keeps the score at the floor of C rather than lower.

#13 Summary conclusion

Vimian has done the hard part of a turnaround. It has a rebuilt leadership team, a growth engine that outruns a shrinking market, and niche positions that protect a high gross margin. Its operating forecasts are among the more predictable parts of this case: demand is chronic, paid in cash and spread across four segments, and our base case needs only what the company has already delivered.

The investment case now turns on conversion, and on the price paid for it. The market has moved first: the multiple has risen by about 40% on unchanged EPS estimates. Consensus expects operating leverage that Vimian's decentralised model does not naturally produce, and below EBITA the costs of buying growth recur. Upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months are therefore likely on revenue and unlikely on EPS.

The case is close to becoming a better one. A cash-and-returns discipline, which the new team could announce as soon as 24 November, would address the weakest part of the foundations, narrow the range of EPS and cash outcomes, and support a multiple nearer the guideline. A lower entry price would improve the risk/reward from the other side. The tests are dated and published: the Capital Markets Day, the inventory and cash figures on 11 February 2027, the Diagnostics margin in April 2027, the organic comparisons in July 2027, and the margin verdict in February 2028.

The four memo ratings

62

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 62, set by the Rater. A strong internal change (64) proven on growth is set against a mild external headwind (41), and the financial output is good but not exceptional: EPS compounds about 16% (A on topic 6) yet part of it comes from bolt-ons and below-the-line relief, with the margin up only about 100bp, so the net force is clearly positive but reaches profits less surely than its revenue effect suggests, in the low 60s with AQ Group and Spie.

56

Foundations' Robustness: 56, set by the Rater. Protected niche moats, chronic and consumable demand that has outgrown a shrinking market every year since 2021 and a stable 69% gross margin give Richard's kind of predictability (as in his Judges Scientific 60), but a quality score of 52 held down by a return on invested capital near 10%, weak cash conversion, a drifting adjusted margin and sponsor-first governance, plus a delivery record of 39 with abandoned targets, keep it below that and well short of CVS Group's top-decile stable margins.

58

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 58, set by the Rater. The case fits 'Delivering - Serial Acquirer - Mechanical EPS Upgrader' in kind (a self-funded bilateral bolt-on engine on durable organic growth) and the Big Corporate Change setup in its rebuilt leadership, but it straddles the two and current problems blur both: the mechanism does not reach EPS after amortisation and earn-outs, and the change has not reached margin, cash or capital allocation (Richard: serial acquirer at 80+ only without problems at the moment); what is already in the price is left to topics 7 and 12.

50

Case Riskiness: 50, set by the Rater. Over a topic 9 score of 44, the operating case is simple and its risks are mostly gradual and published quarterly, which Richard's Arteche 60 shows lifts a case whose main danger is the multiple; it sits below that because EPS is clouded by definitions and acquisition accounting and the share price carries a thin float under a 58% holder with no lock-up and a one-in-seven equity-funded deal risk, so it lands at the middle.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
